title: Advanced Package Workflows: SemVer, Lockfiles, and CI
description: Reason about dependency ranges, reproducible npm installs, scripts and dependency updates in a team repository.
learningOutcomes: Explain dependency ranges versus a locked graph.
Choose npm install, npm ci and npm update appropriately.
Review peer requirements and dependency changes.
Standardize scripts and CI quality gates.
Distinguish bundling, transformation, type checking, linting, formatting and testing responsibilities.

blocks.text: Dependency metadata is part of the project contract

package.json describes direct dependencies, scripts and acceptable version ranges. The lockfile records the resolved dependency graph for the chosen package manager. They work together: changing package.json without a consistent lockfile creates uncertainty, while changing a lockfile without reviewing its diff can bring in unrelated transitive upgrades.

items: `npm install`: installs dependencies and reconciles package metadata/lockfile when declarations change.
`npm ci`: clean automated install from the committed lockfile; requires metadata/lockfile consistency and removes an existing node_modules directory.
`npm update`: intentionally changes resolved packages within allowed ranges; review the lockfile diff and test the resulting graph.
`npm uninstall <name>`: removes a declared package and updates dependency metadata; inspect whether it was direct or transitive first.
`npm run <script>`: runs a named project workflow. Keep documentation and CI aligned with actual package scripts.

steps.title: Ranges express update policy, not the exact dependency graph
steps.explanation: Caret and tilde ranges allow different classes of updates under SemVer rules. The lockfile records the resolved transitive graph.

steps.title: Classify runtime and development dependencies deliberately
steps.explanation: A package belongs in the section appropriate to how the app and deployment actually use it. Do not move dependencies between sections by habit.

steps.title: Make repeatable tasks discoverable
steps.explanation: Named scripts give contributors and CI a shared vocabulary; these are examples, so verify actual script names in the project.

blocks.text: Peer dependencies declare compatibility with a host package such as React. Installation warnings can indicate mismatched major versions; suppressing them blindly may create runtime failures. Before upgrading, check release notes and peer-version ranges, update the lockfile deliberately, then run lint, typecheck, tests and the production build on the resulting commit.

blocks.title: Do not use force as the default conflict resolver
blocks.text: Flags that bypass peer resolution can allow an unsupported package combination to install. Identify the conflicting ranges and choose compatible versions before reaching for a force install.

blocks.prompt: CI needs a clean installation from the committed lockfile and must fail if package metadata and the lockfile disagree. Which command fits?

options.feedback: It performs a clean lockfile-driven install and rejects inconsistent metadata.
Update intentionally changes resolved versions within allowed ranges.

options.text: Delete the lockfile then run npm install
options.feedback: That resolves a fresh dependency tree and undermines reproducibility.
Force can bypass compatibility checks and is not the standard reproducible CI workflow.

blocks.explanation: Use npm ci for CI installs and install/update when deliberately changing dependency resolution.

blocks.title: Review a dependency upgrade like a maintainer
blocks.context: A PR updates a UI library and changes package.json/package-lock.json. Determine whether the change is intentional, compatible and verifiable.
instructions: Inspect both dependency files and classify direct versus transitive changes.
Check the package's supported React peer range and major-version migration notes.
Choose the install command for intentional local dependency changes and for clean CI.
Run or list lint, typecheck, tests and production build gates.
Document the upgrade intent and the behavior tested after the change.
requirements: package.json and the lockfile are reviewed together.
Peer compatibility is checked rather than suppressed by default.
CI installs from the committed lockfile.
Quality gates cover the resulting dependency graph.
The PR explains intent and verification.
blocks.starterCode:
git diff -- package.json package-lock.json

# TODO: inspect direct/transitive changes
# TODO: verify peer ranges and migration notes
npm ci

# TODO: run the actual project scripts
hints: One direct update can change many transitive packages.
Resolve peer conflicts deliberately instead of using --force by default.
Run checks after lockfile changes so tested dependencies match the proposed commit.
successCriteria: Intentional and incidental changes are distinguished.
Install commands suit local changes and CI.
A repeatable verification record is provided.

blocks.text: A frontend toolchain is a set of separate jobs, even when one product supports several of them. The package manager resolves dependencies; a development server serves the app with fast feedback; a bundler builds deployable assets; a compiler/transpiler transforms source; a type checker validates TypeScript types; a linter analyzes code patterns; a formatter lays out code; and a test runner executes tests. Use the actual package scripts as the team contract. Do not repeat a tutorial's blanket claim that Vite is always faster than Webpack: compare the configured workflow and measure the project when performance matters.

blocks.code:
# Inspect package.json, lockfile and the project's configured toolchain first
# For an npm project with a committed package-lock.json:
npm ci

npm run dev

npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm test

npm run build

steps.title: Use the repository's own commands
steps.explanation: Inspect package.json, the matching lockfile and the config before copying commands from a tutorial. `npm ci` fits an npm project with a committed package-lock.json; it is not a generic command for every package manager.

steps.title: Keep static checks separate
steps.explanation: Type checking, linting and tests are independent checks. Vite's TypeScript transformation does not itself type-check the program, so the repository includes an explicit `typecheck` command.

steps.title: Build the production artifact
steps.explanation: The `build` script is the configured production pipeline. In this repository it runs the TypeScript project build before `vite build`; other projects may choose a different sequence.

items: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime used to run local development tools; npm is the package manager commonly installed with Node.js.
Vite combines a development server and production build pipeline. It transforms TypeScript for execution but does not run full TypeScript type checking by itself.

Webpack is an alternative static module bundler built around a dependency graph, with loaders and plugins available for specific transformations and build tasks. A Vite project does not need a second bundler just because a tutorial shows webpack.config.js.
Babel is a JavaScript compiler/toolchain for syntax transforms and compatibility targets; it is not automatically a replacement for a bundler, linter or test runner.
TypeScript's `tsc` checks types. Fast source transformation and full-program type checking are different operations.
ESLint analyzes code for configured correctness and maintainability rules; Prettier formats it. Passing one does not mean the other has run.
This repository uses Vitest for tests. Jest is another test runner, not a command to copy into a project unless its dependencies and scripts are configured for it.
Keep package scripts and the chosen package manager/lockfile aligned; do not maintain competing npm/Yarn lockfiles just to follow two tutorials.

blocks.prompt: A Vite dev server renders the page, but `tsc` reports TypeScript errors. What should a reliable CI pipeline do?

options.text: Run the configured TypeScript check as a separate gate and keep the Vite build
options.feedback: Vite transforms TypeScript for the browser but does not perform full type checking by itself; keep the explicit compiler check.

options.text: Remove the typecheck because a successful dev server proves the types are valid
options.feedback: The dev server can run transformed TypeScript even when the type system would reject the program.

options.text: Replace Vitest with Webpack because a bundler checks TypeScript types
options.feedback: Webpack is a bundler; it does not automatically replace a TypeScript compiler check or a test runner.

options.text: Use Prettier as a substitute for linting and type checking
options.feedback: Prettier formats source code; it does not validate TypeScript types or run behavioral tests.

blocks.explanation: Keep the tool roles and checks separate: transform/build, type checking, linting, formatting and tests answer different questions.

blocks.title: Reconcile a tutorial toolchain with the real repository
blocks.context: A copied tutorial uses Webpack, Babel and Jest, but a repository may already be configured with Vite, TypeScript, Vitest, ESLint and Prettier. Map responsibilities before changing commands or adding dependencies.
instructions: Inspect package.json, the lockfile and the project configuration files before using a tutorial's commands.
Identify which scripts start development, type-check, lint, test, format and build production assets.
For each referenced tool, write its primary responsibility and identify any overlap without treating the tools as interchangeable.
Check whether the documented commands match installed dependencies and the selected package manager.
Propose only the smallest justified change; do not migrate the project to another bundler or test runner merely because a tutorial uses it.
requirements: The package manifest and the chosen lockfile are reviewed together.
Vite transpilation is distinguished from TypeScript type checking.
Webpack and Babel are described by their roles rather than as mandatory extra dependencies.
Lint, format, test and build responsibilities are mapped to actual scripts.
Commands and proposed dependency changes match the repository configuration.
blocks.starterCode:
# Inspect the repository before copying a command block
cat package.json
# TODO: inspect the lockfile and relevant config files

npm ci
npm run typecheck
npm run lint
npm test
npm run build
hints: Start from the repository's scripts; script names are conventions, while the command behind each name determines its behavior.
Vite can transform TypeScript without checking the whole program; check whether the pipeline also invokes tsc.
The presence of a tutorial snippet is not proof that Webpack, Babel or Jest is installed or needed.
successCriteria: Every project command maps to an existing script or is clearly marked as a proposed change.
The selected package manager and lockfile agree.
The pipeline includes the checks relevant to types, code quality, tests and production output.
The toolchain recommendation explains trade-offs without relying on universal performance claims.

items: package.json describes allowed ranges and scripts; the lockfile records the resolved graph.
Use npm ci for reproducible CI, and install/update when intentionally changing resolution.
Review peer compatibility, transitive changes and tests instead of bypassing conflicts with force flags.
